answer.exemplar: The two displays suit different kinds of data, and the deciding question is what was measured. Waiting times are amounts on a scale that can take any value, so they belong in a histogram, where the values are gathered into adjacent intervals of equal width and the bar for an interval covers everything inside it. That is what lets a reader see the shape of a distribution, such as a peak and a tail, and it also means the order and spacing of the intervals carries information. The days of a week are labels, not amounts, and the gap between Tuesday and Wednesday is the same as the gap between Wednesday and Thursday however many customers each had. Bar charts are for those labels, placing one bar per category, and a histogram of them would invent a number line that the labels do not have.

questions.explanation: A histogram is for a measured quantity that runs along a continuous scale, and the crucial feature is that the intervals are adjacent and equal in width, so the area of a bar is what carries the count. A bar chart is for separate categories, where the only thing that matters is which bar is longer and the horizontal positions are just labels with no spacing implied. Putting categories into a histogram therefore suggests a continuity that the categories do not have, since a value halfway between two categories would be a meaningless thing to record. Deciding between the two is a matter of asking whether the horizontal axis measures something or merely names something.
questions.hint: Ask whether the horizontal axis measures an amount that can vary, or only names separate groups.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a histogram suits a measured quantity and a bar chart suits categories

answer.exemplar: A value read off a line of best fit is an estimate because the line is a summary of a direction, not a record of any single case. The line is drawn to sit as near as it can to all the points at once, so it is fitted to the set rather than to any one measurement, and the input asked for often has no point above it at all. That is why the reading is described as a prediction from the trend rather than as an observation. How much the estimate can be trusted comes from the spread of the points around the line, because a tight cluster makes the line a good summary while a wide scatter means a small change in the line would change the estimate a lot. Reporting an estimate to several decimal places is misleading, since the fit does not support that much precision.

questions.explanation: The line is produced by a compromise across the whole set of points, so it is not obliged to agree with any one of them, and the input being estimated may not even appear in the data. That is the sense in which the reading is an estimate rather than a measurement. The spread of the points around the line sets the limit on how precise the reading can be, and it is measured after the line is drawn rather than assumed in advance. Claiming that a best fit must pass through every point confuses summarising a set with describing one member of it, and quoting the estimate to a long string of digits invents a precision the fit never supported.
questions.hint: Separate what the line summarises from what any single measured point records.

answer.exemplar: A circle chart starts from one whole and cuts it into slices, so every question it answers has to be a question about shares of that whole. The size of each slice is found by dividing that part by the total and turning the result into an angle out of 360 degrees, which is why all the shares in a correct circle chart add to the whole and add to 360 degrees at the same time. That is also its limitation, because the chart gives no common baseline to line up the parts, so it is a poor tool for deciding which of several categories is biggest once the slices are all small and similar. A bar chart answers that ranking question directly, and a circle chart answers the share question that a bar chart handles only awkwardly. Choosing wrongly usually means answering a share question with bars, or a ranking question with slices.

questions.explanation: The whole of a circle chart is one total, and each slice is a share of it, so the chart is built to answer part-of-a-whole questions such as what fraction of the total falls in one category. Two slices can be compared by their angles when the difference is large, but once the slices are small and similar the reader has to judge curved boundaries rather than aligned lengths, which is why a bar chart is the better tool for ranking. The shares have to account for the entire circle, and if they add to less than the whole then the chart is either incomplete or has been drawn incorrectly. Reading a bar chart as though the bar lengths were slices gives shares that are measured against the longest bar rather than against the total.
questions.hint: Start from what a circle chart holds constant, which is the total the parts are taken from.

answer.exemplar: A class of 20 students records how many minutes each one read on the day of a test, together with the score that student earned. The 8 students who read 38 minutes or more all scored in the 30s, so the data do support saying that heavier reading and higher scores go together in this class. They do not support saying that reading more minutes produces a higher score, because half of the 12 students who read under 38 minutes also scored in the 30s, so reading time cannot be the only thing moving the score, and one of those students scored 35, which is higher than the scores of 3 of the 8 heavy readers. The claim also cannot be extended past this class, since nothing in the data describes any other group. Settling the cause would need students with the same scores but different reading times, which is not what was recorded here.

questions.explanation: Two separate limits have to be respected, one about cause and one about reach. The first is that a set of paired measurements can show that two things move together without showing that one produces the other, and the second is that a conclusion drawn from one group says nothing about any group the data never covered. Counter-examples inside the data do the work here, since students who read far less and still reached the 30s show that reading time is not the whole story, and the single highest reading is not the single highest score. A claim also fails if the data cannot speak to it at all, which is the case for any statement about students outside the class that was recorded.
questions.hint: Separate what the pairs of numbers show from what they cannot settle, and look inside the data for counter-examples.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a set of paired measurements supports and what it cannot support

questions.explanation: The shares printed on a circle chart account for the whole circle, so the slice with no label is whatever is left after the labelled ones are taken out. The three labelled shares are 45, 30 and 15 percent, and 45 plus 30 plus 15 is 90 percent, so 100 minus 90 leaves 10 percent for the poetry slice. Turning that share into a number of books means taking 10 percent of the total of 400, which is 40. Counting the named slices directly confirms it, since 45 percent of 400 is 180, 30 percent is 120, and 15 percent is 60, and 180 plus 120 plus 60 is 360, leaving 400 minus 360 as 40 books. Reading the 10 as though it were already a number of books would be the standard slip.
